raw_case_text:
A 3-year-old boy was referred to our hospital for left ankle swelling and refusal to walk. A few days before, he had sickness, abdominal pain with vomit, rhinitis, and catarrhal cough. Not traumatic events were reported. His family past illnesses history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed hyperemic pharynx, three small petechiae, respectively on the left buttock, soft palate and chest, a significant swelling of the external peri-malleolar left ankle and of the dorsal region of the left foot, with ecchymotic suffusion and pain on active and passive movements. Ultrasound (US) showed a moderate edema of periarticular soft tissues, without joint effusion or synovial thickening. Blood and urine tests were negative. Nasopharyngeal swabs for SarsCoV2 and group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus were negative, too. After 24 h of observation, his clinical conditions improved, and he was discharged.
Few days later, he was readmitted to our emergency department for a remarkable painful, warm swelling of the back in the paravertebral lumbar region (Figures 1 and 2). Subcutaneous edema of the right ankle and of both knees was also present. Blood and urine tests were negative.
During hospitalization, he presented fleeting swelling with a deep marked migrating livedo.
He required on-demand oral acetaminophen for abdominal pain for a total of five doses. Corticosteroid therapy was not necessary. In the suspect of an angioedema in HSP, an oral antihistaminic therapy was started with partial benefit, so after 72 h was stopped.
Autoimmunity tests were negative and C1q-ihibitor and tryptase serum levels were normal. Platelets count and coagulation tests were in range, except for a moderate reduction of plasma factor XIII activity (53%, n.v: 70%-140%). Nasopharyngeal swab for an enlarged panel of respiratory virus resulted positive for Rhino/Enterovirus. Viral serology for EBV, CMV, Parvovirus B19, Borrelia, Rickettsiae, Leishmania, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative. Fecal occult blood resulted positive in two samples. Coproculture was negative. Urine tests maintained normochromic, without proteinuria. Abdominal US resulted normal; the US of skin and soft tissues showed a minimal imbibition.
The patient never manifested an evident and typical purpuric rash and progressively recovered. He was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of HSP. The planned follow-up is still ongoing.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old boy presented with acute painful left ankle and dorsal foot swelling with refusal to walk, followed a few days later by a large warm painful lumbar paravertebral swelling, bilateral knee and right ankle edema, abdominal pain, and deep migrating livedo.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Several days after an upper respiratory and gastrointestinal prodrome (malaise, abdominal pain, vomiting, rhinitis, and cough), the child presented with left ankle periarticular swelling and refusal to walk, improved transiently within 24 hours, and was readmitted a few days later with a painful warm paravertebral lumbar mass, subcutaneous edema of the right ankle and both knees, intermittent abdominal pain, and fleeting deep migrating livedo without a classic purpuric rash.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy 3-year-old boy with no history of trauma and an unremarkable family medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for preceding rhinitis, cough, vomiting, intermittent abdominal pain, joint/periarticular swelling, lumbar back swelling, and migrating livedo.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: hyperemic pharynx, three small petechiae (on the left buttock, soft palate, and chest), and painful, ecchymotic peri-malleolar left ankle and dorsal left foot swelling limiting active and passive motion. Readmission: marked warm, tender paravertebral lumbar back swelling, subcutaneous edema of the right ankle and both knees, and fleeting deep migrating livedo without classic palpable purpura.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood counts, urinalysis (no hematuria or proteinuria), C1-esterase inhibitor, serum tryptase, autoimmune panel, and standard coagulation tests were normal except for moderately reduced plasma factor XIII activity (53%; ref 70-140%) and two positive fecal occult blood tests. Nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 and Group A Streptococcus, stool cultures, and serologies for Leishmania, EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, Borrelia, Rickettsia, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative, while an extended respiratory viral swab was positive for Rhino/Enterovirus. Ankle, abdominal, and soft-tissue ultrasounds showed moderate periarticular and lumbar subcutaneous soft-tissue edema without joint effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Hereditary angioedema, mastocytosis, and infectious vasculitides (including leishmaniasis, rickettsiosis, borreliosis, and Group A Streptococcus) were excluded; the combination of Rhino/Enterovirus trigger, periarticular and lumbar subcutaneous angioedema, migrating livedo, positive fecal occult blood with abdominal pain, and reduced factor XIII activity (53%) established atypical Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) sine purpura. The child recovered completely with on-demand oral acetaminophen (5 doses) without requiring corticosteroids.
